GridLayout and GridItem — the two components this library exports, plus small utility components.

The package exports these from its main entry point:

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [`GridLayout`](/vue/components/grid-layout/props/) | The grid container — owns the layout array, breakpoints, and collision/compaction logic. |
| [`GridItem`](/vue/components/grid-item/props/) | A single draggable/resizable cell, rendered inside `GridLayout`'s default slot. |
| `CustomCloseButton` | The exact close button `GridItem` renders internally for `showCloseButton` — exported for standalone reuse. See [Styling → GridItem](/vue/components/styling/css-grid-item/). |
| `CustomDragElement` | A standalone drag-handle widget, not used internally by the library — pair it with `GridItem`'s `dragAllowFrom` prop. See [Custom drag handle & close button](/vue/examples/custom-drag-handle-close-button/). |

```ts
import {
  GridLayout,
  GridItem,
  CustomCloseButton,
  CustomDragElement,
} from '@keystone-dashboard-layout/vue';
```

There's no default export — always import by name. See [Installation](/vue/guide/installation/)
if you haven't added the package yet.

- **Drag anywhere, or from a handle.** Every item is draggable by default; restrict it to a specific handle with `dragAllowFrom`, or exclude specific elements with `dragIgnoreFrom`. See [Drag allow/ignore elements](/vue/examples/drag-allow-ignore-elements/) and [Custom drag handle](/vue/examples/custom-drag-handle-close-button/).
- **Resize from any edge or corner** — top, right, bottom, left, and the diagonals — with optional `preserveAspectRatio` locking.
- **Min/max size constraints** (`minW`/`maxW`/`minH`/`maxH`) per item.
- **Bounded dragging** — keep items from being dragged outside the container. See [Bounded drag](/vue/examples/bounded-drag/).
- **Static items** — lock specific items in place; they ignore dragging/resizing entirely and act as fixed obstacles for compaction. See [Static items](/vue/examples/static-items/).
- **Per-item `zIndex` override** — pin one item permanently above every other, including while others are mid-resize, regardless of the library's own implicit static/resizing stacking rules.
- **A separate header region** (`#header` slot) — an optional header area above an item's own main content, its own scrollable region taking whatever space remains.
- **Per-item `autoHeight`** — a live-resyncing height, driven by a real `ResizeObserver` on the item's own content rather than a one-time measurement. See [Per-item autoHeight](/vue/examples/per-item-auto-height/).

## Layout & collision

- **Automatic compaction.** Items fill gaps vertically by default; other items automatically move out of the way of a drag/resize.
- **Pluggable compaction strategy** (`compactType`) — five built-in strategies (vertical, horizontal, none, and overlap variants of each), or replace the algorithm entirely with a custom `ICompactor`. See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/).
- **Horizontal shift mode** — push colliding items left/right instead of down. See [Horizontal shift](/vue/examples/horizontal-shift/).
- **Prevent collision mode** — block a drag/resize instead of pushing other items, with a `MOVE_BLOCKED_BY_COLLISION` event so a consumer can give feedback the moment that happens. See [Prevent collision](/vue/examples/prevent-collision/) and [Blocked-move feedback](/vue/examples/blocked-move-feedback/).
- **Magnetic snap-to-grid** (`snapToGrid`/`snapThreshold`) — actually adjusts an item's landing position to align with a neighbor, not just a visual guide. See [Snap to grid](/vue/examples/snap-to-grid/).
- **Alignment guides** — Figma-style guide lines while dragging or resizing, wherever an item's edges line up with another's. See [Alignment guides while dragging](/vue/examples/alignment-guides/).
- **`restoreOnDrag`** — keep other items from compacting past their pre-drag position while a drag is in progress. See [Layout bounds & rendering options](/vue/examples/layout-bounds-rendering-options/).
- **Auto-sizing container** — the grid's height grows/shrinks to fit its content by default (`autoSize`, or the newer `heightMode` prop for finer control including `'scroll'`/`'fit'` modes). See [Auto-size grid on content](/vue/examples/auto-size-grid/).
- **Spacing indicators** — a labeled distance badge (e.g. "2 cols") in the gap between the active item and its nearest neighbor on each side (`showSpacingGuides`), independently toggleable alongside alignment guides.
- **Serializable layout.** The `layout` array is a plain, JSON-serializable structure you own — persist it anywhere. See [v-model & save/load layout](/vue/examples/save-load-layout/).
- **Named layout presets** (`useLayoutPresets`) — save and switch between multiple named arrangements, layered on the same serialize/restore primitives. See [Named layout presets](/vue/examples/named-presets/).
- **Grid-to-SVG export** (`exportLayoutAsSvg`) — a dependency-free utility producing a standalone SVG snapshot of the current layout. See [Export layout as SVG](/vue/examples/svg-export/).
- **Undo/redo** (`enableUndoRedo`, capped via `undoHistoryLimit`) — opt-in history at committed-change granularity (drag/resize end, add/remove), not per intermediate frame. See [Undo/redo](/vue/examples/undo-redo/).
- **Add/remove items freely**, with automatic re-compaction — no manual position math required. See [Add or remove items](/vue/examples/add-remove-items/).

## Multi-select & group operations

- **Select multiple items** — click to select, Shift/Ctrl/Cmd+click to add additively, click empty background to clear.
- **Group move and resize** — drag or resize any selected item and the rest of the selection moves or resizes by the same delta, from mouse or keyboard alike. See [Multi-select & group move/resize](/vue/examples/multi-select-group-move-resize/).

## Responsive

- **Breakpoint-based column counts**, with sensible defaults (`xxl`/`xl`/`lg`/`md`/`sm`/`xs`/`xxs`) and fully customizable breakpoints/columns. See [Responsive breakpoints](/vue/examples/responsive-breakpoints/).
- **Pre-defined layouts per breakpoint**, for full control over how content reflows instead of relying on auto-generation. See [Responsive predefined layouts](/vue/examples/responsive-predefined-layouts/).

## Internationalization

- **RTL mirroring** for an entire layout or individual items — positions (and dragging) flip horizontally with a single prop. See [Mirrored (RTL)](/vue/examples/mirrored-rtl/).

## Accessibility

- **Keyboard move & resize.** Every non-static, editable item is keyboard-focusable — arrow keys move it, Shift+arrow keys resize it — without needing any extra configuration. Reuses the exact same events/collision handling the mouse-driven path uses. See [Accessibility scope](/vue/guide/project/accessibility/) for the full scope, including what's deliberately not (yet) covered.
- **Screen reader support** — interactive items are announced with `role="group"` and a description of the available keyboard controls; visible focus indicator for keyboard users.
- **Localizable ARIA strings** (`ariaLabels`) — the close button's label, `aria-roledescription`, and the keyboard move/resize instructions are overridable (`GridLayout` grid-wide default, `GridItem` per-item override), rather than hardcoded English literals. ## Multi-select

Off by default (`multiSelect: false`) — every prior behavior is
completely unaffected when this stays off. When on:

- **Click** an item — selects only it, replacing any prior selection.
- **Shift+click or Ctrl/Cmd+click** — adds/removes that item from the
  current selection additively.
- **Click empty grid background** — clears the selection entirely.

Dragging or resizing any *selected* item while more than one item is
selected moves/resizes every other selected item by the same delta —
also works from the keyboard (arrow keys/Shift+arrow on a focused,
selected item), not just mouse/touch drag.

A passenger that's static, or has `isDraggable`/`isResizable`
explicitly `false`, never moves or resizes as part of a group gesture
— the same guarantee a static item already has against the normal
collision-push cascade. A passenger's own `minW`/`maxW`/`minH`/`maxH`
are also respected individually during group resize, not just clamped
to the anchor's own limits (or a bare floor of 1) — see item "d" in the
demo above, which stops at its own `maxW` of 3 even while the other,
unconstrained items keep growing.

:::caution[Deliberately scoped, not fully collision-aware]
The delta is applied directly to every other selected item's position
or size — there's no per-passenger collision detection against
*non-selected* items during the gesture itself, only the
dragged/resized item gets the usual collision/bounds handling.
Compaction (per `compactType`) still runs normally once the
gesture ends.
:::

Listen for `@selection-changed` (payload: the full current selection as
an array) to react to selection changes, or read the exposed
`selectedItems` directly.

The internal event bus GridLayout and GridItem use to talk to each other.

`GridLayout` and every `GridItem` communicate through a shared,
named-event bus — `GridLayout` creates it (via an in-house
`createEventEmitter()` helper, not a third-party library) and provides
it; every `GridItem` injects it. This is internal plumbing, not part of
the public component API, but understanding it helps when debugging why
a prop change on `GridLayout` did or didn't reach an item.

What KeystoneGrid for Vue is, what you get, and where to go next.

KeystoneGrid for Vue is a Vue 3 component library for building
draggable, resizable, responsive dashboard grids — the kind of UI you'd
use for a customizable analytics dashboard, a widget board, or any screen
where users rearrange content themselves.

It's a TypeScript-first library built from the ground up on Vue 3's
Composition API, using a native, Pointer Events-based drag/resize engine
with no third-party runtime dependency for it at all.

## What you get

- **`GridLayout`** — the container. Owns the layout array (position/size
  of every item), responsive breakpoint state, and collision/compaction
  logic.
- **`GridItem`** — a single draggable/resizable cell, rendered inside
  `GridLayout`'s default slot. You control what's inside it — text,
  images, charts, forms, anything.
- **Two small utility components** — `CustomCloseButton` and
  `CustomDragElement` — exported in case you want to reuse the library's
  own default close button or build a dedicated drag handle.

## How it fits together

```vue
<GridLayout v-model:layout="layout">
  <GridItem v-for="item in layout" :key="item.i" v-bind="item">
    <!-- your content -->
  </GridItem>
</GridLayout>
```

`layout` is a plain array of `{ i, x, y, w, h, ... }` objects — one per
`GridItem`. You own that array; the library reads and updates it as the
user drags and resizes things. Everything else (collision resolution,
compaction, responsive breakpoint switching) happens automatically based
on the props you set.

## Design goals

A few decisions that shape how the library behaves, worth knowing up
front:

- **You own the data.** The layout array is yours — the library mutates
  it in place / emits updates, but never hides state you can't inspect or
  serialize (see [v-model & save/load layout](/vue/examples/save-load-layout/)).
- **Sensible defaults, explicit overrides.** Most behavior (draggable,
  resizable, bounded, etc.) can be set once on `GridLayout` and inherited
  by every item, or overridden per-item when needed.
- **Composition over configuration objects.** Props map directly to
  documented, individually-typed options rather than one large opaque
  config object — better autocomplete, better documentation per option.

The same shared event bus documented on

## Listens for (pushed down from GridLayout)

`changeDirection`, `compact`, `setBounded`, `setBorderRadiusPx`,
`setColNum`, `setDraggable`, `setEnableEditMode`, `setMargin`,
`setMaxRows`, `setResizable`, `setResizeHandles`, `setRowHeight`,
`setShowCloseButton`, `setTransformScale`, `setUseBorderRadius`,
`setUseCssTransforms`, `updateWidth` — each has a corresponding handler
registered on mount and deregistered on unmount.

The `setDraggable`/`setResizable`/`setBounded`/`setShowCloseButton`/
`setEnableEditMode`/`setUseBorderRadius`/`setBorderRadiusPx`/
`setResizeHandles` handlers only apply the pushed value when the item's
own matching prop is `null` — an explicit per-item prop always wins
over the cascade. `setUseCssTransforms` is the one exception: it applies
unconditionally, since there's no per-item override for it at all.

## Emits (reported up to GridLayout)

`dragEvent` and `resizeEvent`, both carrying an `IEventsData` payload —
emitted on every `dragstart`/`dragmove`/`dragend` (or
`resizestart`/`resizemove`/`resizeend`) tick. `itemClicked` (an
`IItemClickedData` payload) fires on a genuine click/tap, backing
`GridLayout`'s own `multiSelect` handling.

See [GridLayout's eventbus events](/vue/components/grid-layout/eventbus-events/)
for the full message table and payload shapes.

Emitted directly on a `<GridItem>` — listen with `@event-name`.

| Event | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `container-resized` | `(i, h, w, height, width)` | The item's rendered pixel size changed. See [Layout lifecycle events](/vue/examples/layout-lifecycle-events/). |
| `item-clicked` | `(i, event: MouseEvent)` | A genuine click/tap on the item — the trailing click a browser can still dispatch immediately after a drag/resize gesture ends is suppressed. The native `MouseEvent` is included so a handler can check `shiftKey`/`ctrlKey`/`metaKey`. Backs `GridLayout`'s own `multiSelect` handling. See [Multi-select & group move/resize](/vue/examples/multi-select-group-move-resize/). |
| `item-move` | `(i, x, y)` | Fired continuously while a drag is in progress, whenever the grid-unit position changes. |
| `item-moved` | `(i, x, y)` | Fired once when a drag completes and the position actually changed. |
| `remove-grid-item` | `(i)` | The item's close button was clicked. See [Show close button](/vue/examples/close-button/). |

## Resize direction support

All four edges — top, right, bottom, left — and their diagonal corners
are resizable. Left/top-edge resizes move the item's position (`x`/`y`)
as well as its size, since growing from the left/top edge means the
opposite edge stays fixed. In RTL mode, this is mirrored correctly too —
dragging the right edge (rather than the left) is what moves the
anchor. See [Mirrored (RTL)](/vue/examples/mirrored-rtl/).

  background: #0f172a;

## `.vue-grid-layout--active-drag`

Applied only while a cross-grid drag (`allowCrossGridDrag`) is in
progress, bumping this grid's own `z-index` to `1` — a real fix for a
real bug: with every grid establishing its own CSS stacking context
(`isolation: isolate`, needed separately so a negative-`z-index` static
item doesn't escape its own grid's subtree), a dragged item paints
behind whichever sibling grid happens to come later in the DOM, unless
its own source grid's stacking context is temporarily raised above its
siblings during the drag. Not meant to be restyled — documented here so
an unexpectedly-elevated `z-index` during a cross-grid drag isn't a
mystery if you notice it in devtools.

Grid line guides (`showGridLines`) are **not** controlled by a SCSS
variable at all, despite an earlier version of this page claiming
otherwise as `$grid-line-color`. Checked directly against
`GridLayout.vue`'s own `<style>` block: the actual mechanism is a real

.vue-grid-layout {

What keyboard and screen-reader support KeystoneGrid for Vue actually provides — and what it deliberately doesn't (yet).

Before keyboard support was added, there was no way to move or resize a
`GridItem` other than a mouse or touch drag. For a library whose entire
purpose is letting end users rearrange a layout, that's a real gap, not a
nice-to-have.

## What's implemented

### Keyboard move and resize

Every non-static, editable `GridItem` is keyboard-focusable
(`tabindex="0"`) and operable:

- **Arrow keys** move it by one grid unit, if it's draggable.
- **Shift + arrow keys** resize it by one grid unit, if it's resizable.

Each keypress is treated as a complete, atomic gesture — there's no
keyboard equivalent of a continuous drag to preview mid-way through —
and emits the same event pairs and eventBus messages the mouse-driven
path already uses, so compaction and collision handling apply
identically regardless of which input method triggered the change.

**Works with `multiSelect`'s group move/resize too** — arrow-key/
Shift+arrow movement on a focused, *selected* item moves/resizes every
other selected item by the same delta, the same as a mouse/touch drag
already does. See [Multi-select & group move/resize](/vue/examples/multi-select-group-move-resize/).

**Deliberately scoped to single-unit steps**, not a full
[WAI-ARIA grid](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/grid/) or
[application](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) widget pattern
(roving `tabindex` between cells, a distinct "move mode" toggle key,
etc.). This library isn't a traditional data grid — it's a freeform
draggable canvas — so the full APG grid pattern doesn't map cleanly onto
it. The goal was closing the actual gap (no keyboard alternative existed
at all), not redesigning the interaction model.

### Screen reader support

- Each interactive item gets `role="group"` and
  `aria-roledescription="Draggable, resizable item"`, so a screen reader
  announces it as something other than a plain, silent `<div>`.
- `aria-describedby` points to a visually-hidden instructions string
  ("Press arrow keys to move." / "Press shift plus arrow keys to
  resize.", each only included if that action actually applies to the
  item) — discoverable on focus, not a mandatory upfront announcement.
- A visible focus outline, so a keyboard user can actually see which
  item currently has focus.

### A deliberate, non-obvious design decision worth calling out

Keyboard move/resize **ignores `dragAllowFrom`/`dragIgnoreFrom`/
`resizeIgnoreFrom`** entirely — those props restrict which DOM element a
*mouse* drag/resize gesture can originate from (see
[Drag allow/ignore elements](/vue/examples/drag-allow-ignore-elements/) and
[Custom drag handle](/vue/examples/custom-drag-handle-close-button/)),
which is a concept that doesn't map onto keyboard interaction at all —
there's no "which element did the keypress originate from" equivalent to
"which element did the mousedown originate from." A keyboard user who
focuses the item gets full move/resize access regardless of whether a
mouse user is restricted to a specific handle. This is intentional, not
an oversight: restricting keyboard users *further* than mouse users, just
because a mouse-specific UI affordance (a drag handle) exists, would be
the wrong direction for an accessibility feature to take.

### Localizable ARIA strings

The close button's label, `aria-roledescription`, and the keyboard
move/resize instructions are all overridable rather than hardcoded
English literals — see [Localizable ARIA strings](/vue/examples/aria-labels/).

## What's not covered (tracked, not silently ignored)

- **No roving-tabindex grid navigation.** Tabbing moves through items in
  DOM order (which usually, but not necessarily, matches visual order),
  the same as any other focusable elements on a page — there's no
  arrow-key-based "move focus to the item above/below/left/right"
  navigation independent of actually moving the focused item. That's part
  of the full APG grid pattern this deliberately doesn't implement.
- **No keyboard equivalent for the drag-from-outside / drag-between-grids
  examples** ([Drag, drop from outside](/vue/examples/outside-drag-drop/),
  [Drag, drop from grid to grid](/vue/examples/cross-grid-drag-drop/)) —
  those are consumer-level example code, not library internals, and
  would need their own keyboard handling written the same way the
  examples currently write their own mouse handling.
- **Not independently audited against WCAG success criteria** or run
  through an automated tool (axe, Lighthouse, etc.) — what's implemented
  was reasoned through manually against the specific gap found (no
  keyboard alternative), not verified against a full checklist. A real
  automated accessibility audit is a reasonable next step, and would
  likely find things this pass didn't.
- **Color contrast and the default item styling generally** haven't been
  reviewed — `GridItem`'s content is unstyled by default (see
  [Styling → GridItem](/vue/components/styling/css-grid-item/)), so this
  is mostly a consumer responsibility, but the library's own default
  close button and focus outline colors haven't been explicitly checked
  against contrast ratios.

How GridLayout and GridItem talk to each other, and how the codebase is organized.

The map worth knowing before digging deeper into how the library is
built — `GridLayout` and `GridItem` carry almost the entire
implementation, and their relationship isn't obvious from reading either
file in isolation.

## Two entry points

The main package entry (`GridLayout`, `GridItem`, and everything that
needs a live component instance or DOM) is one thing; a separate
`/core` subpath export is the pure grid-layout math those components are
built on — collision detection, compaction, movement, alignment guides,
breakpoint resolution, serialization, and validation — with zero Vue
dependency and no live DOM required. Useful standalone, e.g. for
validating a layout server-side.

`/core` ships as its own build (`es`/`cjs` only), separate from the main
library's build (which still needs a UMD output for script-tag/CDN
consumers, and Vite doesn't support multiple entry points when `umd` is
one of the output formats).

## Pluggable compaction

Every compaction call (drag end, resize end, mount, breakpoint change,
`compactNow()`) routes through one internal helper, which checks the
`compactor` prop first, falling back to whichever of the five built-in
strategies `compactType` selects. `compactor: null` (the default) means
"use whichever built-in strategy `compactType` selects" — a purely
additive override, not a replacement for that prop. All five built-in
strategies are exported from both the main entry and `/core`, as a
starting point for writing a custom one. See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/).

## Undo/redo

Opt-in, snapshot-at-committed-change granularity, not per intermediate
drag-move frame. The pre-mutation layout is captured explicitly at
`dragstart`/`resizestart` and committed at `dragend`/`resizeend` — after
the position update and compaction have already run — rather than
reading a single shared "last known state" implicitly at commit time,
which would only ever see "nothing's changed yet" if read too early in
the gesture. See [Undo/redo](/vue/examples/undo-redo/).

## How GridLayout and GridItem talk to each other

A consumer renders `GridItem`s themselves, inside `GridLayout`'s default
slot — `GridLayout` doesn't create your items for you. It creates
exactly one extra, hidden `GridItem` internally: the drag placeholder
shown while dragging or resizing.

Communication runs two ways:

### `$parent`

`GridItem` reads its parent instance directly, which works because it's
always rendered as a direct child of `GridLayout`'s template. This is a
**one-time snapshot at mount**, not a live reactive reference — a later
change to a `GridLayout` prop won't be reflected through this path no
matter how many times it's read. Anything that needs to reach an
already-mounted `GridItem` after the fact uses the eventBus below
instead.

### The eventBus

`GridLayout` provides an event emitter that every `GridItem` injects —
the direction for `GridLayout` pushing targeted updates down to
potentially many items at once (rather than re-rendering every item on
every relevant change), and for items reporting drag/resize activity
back up. Cascading settings like `isDraggable`/`isResizable`/`isBounded`/
`showCloseButton` propagate this way — each only applied by an item
whose own prop is left at its inherit-from-parent default.

## Inside GridItem: composable split

`GridItem`'s own drag, resize, and keyboard-interaction logic each live
in their own composable rather than one large file — genuinely coupled
(drag/resize act on the same DOM element via the same native
pointer-driven engine; keyboard deliberately reuses drag/resize's own
resolved state and event paths, so the same collision/compaction
handling already tested against the mouse path applies to keyboard
input with no separate handling needed on `GridLayout`'s side at all),
but each still gets its own file, name, and test surface.

## Native drag/resize engine

Both drag and resize wire up a native, Pointer Events-based engine once
per `GridItem` — no third-party drag/resize library at all. Unlike an
approach that needs re-invoking on every relevant prop/state change to
reconfigure, this engine reads its own current options fresh on every
`pointerdown`, so the wiring only needs to happen once. Each gesture is
guarded to one pointer at a time per element, so a second concurrent
pointer (two fingers, an accidental palm touch mid-drag) can't silently
hijack tracking.

## Cross-grid drag/drop

`allowCrossGridDrag` needs separate `GridLayout` instances — frequently
with no Vue ancestor/descendant relationship to each other at all — to
find one another. A plain, module-level registry (not Vue reactive
state, not provide/inject) is the answer: every participating grid
registers itself on mount and deregisters on unmount; the only lookup
either side needs is a scan over whatever's currently registered, fine
at the scale this feature operates at. See [Drag, drop from grid to grid](/vue/examples/cross-grid-drag-drop/).

## Outside drag/drop

Architecturally the simplest of the three drag-related features, since
it's the only one that never needs to coordinate with anything else — a
grid with `allowOutsideDrop` set only cares about drags happening
directly over its own root element, from a source it has no ongoing
relationship with before or after the drop. Reuses the same
placeholder/dragging state a normal in-grid drag already drives, rather
than a second, parallel preview mechanism. See [Drag, drop from outside](/vue/examples/outside-drag-drop/).

## Responsive breakpoints and alignment guides

The per-breakpoint layout cache, the currently active breakpoint, and
the function that finds or generates the right layout for the current
container width all live together, since the coupling there is narrow.
Alignment guides are simpler still — a pure function (given the active
item's live position/size and the rest of the layout, returns which
edges align) called from the existing drag/resize hook points, not a
separate composable or watcher of its own.

## Testing implications

`GridLayout` and `GridItem` are tested together, mounting a real
`GridLayout` with real `GridItem` children in its slot — the only way to
exercise the `$parent`/eventBus contract the way production actually
uses it. Testing `GridItem` with a hand-rolled fake parent would
validate a contract that might not match what `GridLayout` actually
provides. See [Testing philosophy](/vue/guide/project/testing/) for the fuller picture.
How KeystoneGrid for Vue compares to Kendo TileLayout and DevExtreme's Dashboard Designer.

## Scope, and why this is separate from Comparison: alternatives

[Comparison: alternatives](/vue/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/)
scopes itself to open-source peers in the same category. This page
covers two commercial products instead, kept separate since both the
licensing model and (for one of the two) the actual product category
differ enough that folding them into the same table would be
misleading.

Two things worth correcting up front: Kendo's actual component is
called **TileLayout** (available for jQuery, Angular, React, and
Blazor) — "DashboardLayout" isn't a real Kendo product name. And
DevExtreme's **Dashboard Designer** is a full BI platform, not a
standalone layout component — it bundles data source binding,
drill-down interactivity, a WYSIWYG designer, and export around its own
layout mechanism. This page compares against just its layout engine
(the drag/resize/arrange mechanics), since that's the only part in the
same category as this library.

## The bigger architectural difference

Both commercial products use a **recursive binary split-pane tree**:
adding a new item splits the largest existing pane in half; resizing
means dragging the separator line between two adjacent panes, not
independent per-item resize handles — the same model as a tiling window
manager or an IDE's split editor panes. This library uses **freeform,
independent `x`/`y`/`w`/`h` grid coordinates** instead: any item can
move to any free position on its own, with its own resize handles on
its own edges.

This isn't a minor detail — several rows below aren't simple
"missing feature" gaps, they're different tradeoffs a different
architecture makes. A split-pane tree structurally guarantees no
overlaps and no compaction step, at the cost of items never being fully
independent of their neighbors. Freeform coordinates give full
independent placement, at the cost of needing an explicit
collision/compaction system. Neither is strictly better; they suit
different products.

| Click-to-select, click-to-place reorder (no drag gesture) | No | **Yes** — a real, non-drag accessibility alternative worth considering here | No |
| Vue support | Native, ground-up | **None** — jQuery, Angular, React, Blazor only | Via a wrapper layer over a shared core |
| Licensing | MIT, free | Commercial, but free for the React build specifically | Commercial, no free tier |

| Drag-and-drop from outside the component | Yes | No | No — Toolbox is click-to-add, not a drag gesture |
| Responsive breakpoints | Yes | No | Auto-stretches to fit its container — a different, non-breakpoint mechanism |

## Honest summary

Against **Kendo TileLayout**: this library is ahead on nearly every
drag/resize/layout-mechanics dimension — full 8-edge independent resize
vs. a 3-handle/axis-restricted model, freeform positioning vs.
reorder-only, cross-grid drag, outside drop, snap/alignment guides,
undo/redo, multi-select. TileLayout's genuine advantages: being one
component in a large commercial suite with paid support, a mature
click-move-click accessibility mode this library doesn't have, and
(for the React build specifically) being free. There's no Vue build to
compare against directly at all.

Against **DevExtreme Dashboard**: these aren't real competitors for
most consumers — Dashboard Designer is a BI-authoring product where
drag/resize layout is one supporting piece of a much larger
data-analytics platform, not something you'd choose *for* its layout
engine alone. The one genuine, worth-tracking gap even at the pure
layout-mechanics level is **maximize/restore** — a common, useful
dashboard pattern this library doesn't have. It's tracked on the
[Roadmap](/vue/guide/project/roadmap/), not yet designed.

## What's not worth chasing from either

- **Kendo's CSS Grid-based, resize-restricted-to-3-handles model** —
  adopting this would be a regression, not a gap to close.
- **DevExtreme's recursive split-pane structure itself** — rebuilding
  around that architecture would abandon the freeform positioning model
  that's core to what this library is. If a split-pane mode is ever
  genuinely wanted, it belongs as an alternative, opt-in mode, not a
  replacement.
- **DevExtreme's BI/data-analytics layer entirely** — a different
  product category by design, not a scope this library is trying to
  grow into.

Two independent test layers.

## Unit & component tests — Vitest

Pure-function tests for the grid math, validators, and helpers, plus
component tests for every Vue component (`GridLayout`, `GridItem`,
`CustomCloseButton`, `CustomDragElement`), all run against jsdom.

```sh
npm run test           # watch mode
npm run test:ui         # Vitest UI
npm run test:coverage   # single run with coverage
```

### Coverage gate

A **90% minimum** (lines, statements, functions, branches) is enforced
over the library's own source, excluding pure type-declaration files
(interfaces/types have no emitted JS to cover) and the demo app. A run
that drops below 90% on any of those four metrics fails — the same gate
CI runs. See [Production readiness](/vue/guide/project/production-readiness/) for the current real numbers.

### Component testing approach

`GridLayout` and `GridItem` are tested together, mounted so that a real
`GridLayout` renders real `GridItem` children in its default slot — the
same shape actual usage takes. This means `$parent` and the eventBus
(see [Architecture](/vue/guide/project/architecture/)) behave exactly as
they do in production, rather than relying on a hand-rolled fake parent.

A few things need mocking, since jsdom can't provide them:

- **`ResizeObserver`** — jsdom doesn't implement it at all. Replaced
  with a no-op stub for most tests; the initial container-width
  measurement is handled separately.
- **The native drag/resize engine's own pointer handling** — real,
  trusted pointer events and native layout aren't something jsdom can
  produce faithfully. Tests invoke the component's actual drag/resize
  handling logic directly (via a small test backdoor the native engine
  exposes for exactly this), rather than trying to simulate a full,
  real mouse gesture through jsdom.
- **Vue's `useSlots()`**, scoped to the `autoHeight`/`autoSize()` test
  file only — the "happy path" of measuring a slot's actual mounted
  element can't be reached through ordinary Vue slot rendering in a
  test, since calling the exposed `slots.default()` imperatively returns
  fresh, disconnected VNodes regardless. This is the one place a
  targeted mock is the only way to exercise that logic at all.

Testing a `GridItem`'s own prop watchers needs a slightly different
mounting approach than testing the root component directly, since
`GridItem` is rendered through `GridLayout`'s slot rather than as the
test's own root — the project's own test helpers mount with the item's
props on a reactive object instead, so mutating that object re-renders
`GridItem` with new props exactly like a real `v-for` over reactive
state would.

## End-to-end tests — Playwright

Browser tests that drive real drag/resize/responsive interactions
against a real demo app, across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.

```sh
npx playwright install   # first time only — downloads browser binaries
npm run test:e2e          # headless, all three browser engines
npm run test:e2e:ui       # interactive UI mode, good for writing new tests
npm run test:e2e:report   # open the HTML report from the last run
```

### What's covered

| Area | Covers |
|---|---|
| Basic grid | Static layout renders at the right positions; default draggable/resizable classes are applied |
| Drag & resize | Dragging moves an item and fires the move event; disabling `isDraggable` blocks movement; resizing from the bottom-right edge grows an item |
| Keyboard accessibility | Arrow-key move and shift+arrow resize; boundary clamping; min-size clamping on shrink; a non-interactive item ignores keyboard input entirely |
| Dynamic items | Adding a layout entry renders a new item; the close button removes one |
| Responsive | Shrinking the viewport moves the layout to a narrower breakpoint |
| External drop | Dragging a native element from outside into one of two grids lands it in whichever grid it was released over; releasing away from both grids drops nothing; a single continuous drag swept from one grid to the other leaves exactly one preview; an existing item can also be dragged between grids via `allowCrossGridDrag` |
| Advanced features | Blocked-move feedback (`preventCollision` + a static item), `compactNow()` re-packing a scattered layout, `duplicateItem`, `snapToGrid` magnetic alignment, saving/loading a named layout preset |

### Notes on interaction tests

Drag and resize tests drive real pointer input (mouse down → move in
steps → up) rather than clicking a locator, since the native engine
needs a real sequence of pointer events to recognize a drag/resize
gesture — a single click won't trigger it.

Resize specifically is edge-triggered (grabbing near the item's own
border, not a separate handle element for most cases), so resize tests
grab a point a couple of pixels inside the item's corner rather than
clicking a dedicated handle.

A container-width measurement can settle across more than one render
pass after mount or a view switch — waiting for an item's own
"draggable-ready" class confirms the drag engine's setup has run, but
not that the container's own width measurement has also finished. A
shared "stable bounding box" test helper exists specifically to avoid
reading a position mid-settle, after this was found to affect even
previously-solid tests, not just newly-added ones.

## Manual testing

Neither Vitest nor the e2e suite covers everything. Cross-browser
scenarios with zero automated coverage in this project's current
environment, touch/mobile behavior, and screen-reader scenarios all
need a human in a real browser — tracked in a manual test checklist, run
before a release touching drag/resize/collision logic, or quarterly
otherwise.

## What's still open

### A Nuxt module, paired with a real SSR audit

One concrete SSR-breaking spot (an unguarded `navigator.userAgent` read
inside a template-bound computed) has already been found and fixed —
but that was one specific instance checked, not the exhaustive sweep a
real audit would need before shipping a dedicated Nuxt wrapper around
the rest of the codebase.

### Swap-on-drag collision mode

Dragging item A onto item B swaps their positions, as an alternative to
the current push-aside compaction. Common in consumer tile-dashboard
products (see [Comparison: alternatives](/vue/guide/project/comparison-alternatives/)
for how `gridstack.js` handles this today).

### Maximize/restore an item

Temporarily expand a single item to fill the grid's entire visible
area (its own header/close button still reachable, everything else
hidden without being removed from `layout`), then restore it to its
prior position/size. Needs its own design pass before starting,
particularly around what happens to *other* items' compaction while one
is maximized, and whether this lives as a per-item prop/method or a
grid-level "which item is currently maximized" state. See
[Comparison: commercial](/vue/guide/project/comparison-commercial/) for
where this idea came from (DevExtreme's Dashboard Designer has it;
Kendo TileLayout doesn't).

### Async persistence backends

A new, separate composable with its own adapter interface for IndexedDB
and remote-HTTP-backed persistence, alongside (not replacing) the
existing synchronous storage helper. `sessionStorage` already works
today via the existing helper's own storage option — not a gap needing
new code.

### An open, pluggable CSS positioning strategy

An interface (mirroring the existing pluggable-compaction precedent)
replacing the current on/off toggle between CSS transforms and
`top`/`left` positioning, with both current behaviors preserved as
built-ins.

### A fast, large-layout compaction algorithm

An additional compaction strategy, implementing the same pluggable
interface as the built-in ones, aimed at very large layouts. Needs a
real performance benchmark proving the complexity claim before shipping
— not to be added as an unverified swap.

### A worker-based layout engine

An opt-in Web Worker executor for compaction/responsive-generation on
very large layouts. The largest lift of anything on this list —
deliberately deferred until the fast-compaction item above alone is
proven insufficient on its own, not built speculatively alongside it.

Keyboard support is deliberately scoped to single-unit-step move/resize,

## Scope

This compares projects in the same category as this library —
**draggable/resizable dashboard layout engines** (position arbitrary
widgets on a grid, drag/resize them, responsive breakpoints) — not data
tables/grids (Kendo's Grid, AG Grid, etc.), which solve a different
problem. For commercial layout-engine peers, see
[Comparison: commercial](/vue/guide/project/comparison-commercial/) instead.

Projects compared: **`vue-grid-layout`** (jbaysolutions, the original
Vue library this space descends from), **`grid-layout-plus`** (a Vue 3
migration of the original, now the closest thing to a de-facto default
by real npm download volume), **`react-grid-layout`** (the React
equivalent this whole category traces back to, recently rewritten with
a hooks-based v2), and **`gridstack.js`** (framework-agnostic, ships
official Vue/React/Angular wrappers).

## The headline finding

The most-starred Vue option, `vue-grid-layout`, still has no official
Vue 3 release years after Vue 3 shipped — its own issue tracker confirms
people were still asking about a Vue 3 alternative well after Vue 3's
release. What filled the gap instead is a scatter of independently
maintained community forks with no single obvious default among
them — except that one of them, `grid-layout-plus`, has actually
emerged as something close to a de-facto default by real usage: an
order of magnitude more weekly downloads than the other forks, its own
polished documentation site, and a regular release history. It's a
faithful Vue 3 port of the original codebase, not an expanded fork — its
own feature set matches the original almost exactly, nothing more.

## Where this project genuinely leads

Cross-referencing the table above, the features with **no equivalent in
any alternative checked**: magnetic snap-to-grid (distinct from a
visual guide), visual alignment guides, the blocked-move feedback
event, named layout presets, grid-to-SVG export, localizable ARIA
strings as a dedicated prop surface, live-resyncing per-item
`autoHeight`, and multi-select with group move/resize. None of these
are exotic — they're the kind of real-world friction points (hand-rolled
persistence, a hand-wired collision-shake animation, English-only
screen reader text) a dedicated roadmap process exists specifically to
find and close one at a time.

## Where this project is genuinely behind

- **Ecosystem size and battle-testing.** `react-grid-layout` and
  `gridstack.js` have years more production usage across far more
  companies — not a feature gap this library can close by writing code,
  just a newer project.
- **Framework breadth.** `gridstack.js` covers Vue, React, and Angular
  from one core engine. This library is Vue-only by design today — a
  reasonable scope choice, but a real limitation for a team needing the
  same layout logic across multiple frameworks (see the
  [landing page](/)'s own React/Angular framework picker for where that's headed).
- **Sub-grids / nesting.** `gridstack.js` supports grids-within-grids as
  first-class nested structures. This library's cross-grid feature is
  sibling-to-sibling dragging between independent grid instances — a
  different capability, not a nesting system.
- **Swap-on-drag.** In `gridstack.js`'s default top-gravity mode,
  dragging one item onto another of the same size swaps their
  positions. This library only pushes items aside via compaction — an
  item landing on another never swaps with it.
- **A specific, unusually feature-rich fork** (`@marsio/vue-grid-layout`,
  minimal current adoption but technically ambitious) offers multiple
  persistence backends and a worker-based layout engine for very large
  layouts, neither of which this project has yet (both are on the
  [Roadmap](/vue/guide/project/roadmap/)). It does **not**, however,
  have an equivalent to several things this project already checked and
  confirmed it does have, contrary to an earlier version of this
  comparison: align/distribute commands over a multi-selection
  (`alignSelected`/`distributeSelected`, exposed on the `GridLayout`
  instance), a configurable resize-handle *set* (`resizeHandles`,
  restricting which specific corners/edges render, not just an
  all-or-nothing toggle), and spacing guides with distance labels
  (`showSpacingGuides`). The fork in turn has no equivalent to this
  project's cross-grid drag, outside-drop typed-payload helper, or
  multi-select **group resize** specifically (its own docs note group
  move is supported but group resize is not).

## Bottom line

For a Vue 3, TypeScript-first dashboard layout library, the realistic
field is small and genuinely fragmented — the most-starred option still
doesn't officially support Vue 3, and what exists instead is a handful
of differently-maintained community forks with no clear default.
Measured against that actual field, this project has meaningfully more
features (several with no equivalent in any alternative checked) and a
more rigorously documented test/coverage process, at the cost of being
a newer, smaller-community project without the multi-year production
track record the category's oldest entries can claim.

## Pairing with `resizeIgnoreFrom`

If the handle sits near a corner, it can land inside the same
edge-proximity margin the resize engine already uses to detect a resize
gesture — meaning grabbing the handle could start a resize instead of
the drag `dragAllowFrom` was meant to restrict things to. Excluding the
handle from `resizeIgnoreFrom` as well is what actually stops the two
from fighting over the same gesture:

```vue
<GridItem
  drag-allow-from=".vue-draggable-handle"
  resize-ignore-from=".vue-draggable-handle"
  ...>
```

See [Custom drag handle & close button](/vue/examples/custom-drag-handle-close-button/)
for a full working example combining this with `CustomCloseButton`.

One entry in a GridLayout's layout array — every field a layout item can carry.

One entry in a `GridLayout`'s `layout` array. The optional fields mirror
the corresponding `GridItem` props (`isDraggable`, `minH`, etc.) —
Vue's own `GridItem` takes most of these as direct component props
rather than reading them from the layout item, so setting one here is
mainly useful for configuring items from data instead of template props.

```ts
interface ILayoutItemRequired {
  i: string | number;
  h: number;
  w: number;
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

interface ILayoutItem<TMeta = unknown> extends ILayoutItemRequired {
  // ...optional fields below
}
```

`ILayoutItemRequired` is exported separately too, in case you need to
type just the required fields on their own (a minimal seed object before
optional fields are added, say).

## Required fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `i` | `string \| number` | Unique identifier, matched against a `GridItem`'s `i` prop. |
| `h` | `number` | Height, in grid row units. |
| `w` | `number` | Width, in grid column units. |
| `x` | `number` | Horizontal position, in grid column units. |
| `y` | `number` | Vertical position, in grid row units. |

## Optional fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `isDraggable` | `boolean` | Per-item drag override. |
| `isResizable` | `boolean` | Per-item resize override. |
| `isStatic` | `boolean` | Excludes this item from dragging, resizing, and collision cascades. |
| `maxH` / `maxW` / `minH` / `minW` | `number` | Per-item size constraints. |
| `zIndex` | `number \| null` | CSS `z-index` override, winning over the static/dragging/resizing CSS-class defaults. |
| `showCloseButton` | `boolean` | Per-item override; `undefined` defers to the grid-wide default. |
| `autoScroll` | `boolean` | Per-item override for native auto-scroll near a container edge during drag/resize. |
| `preserveAspectRatio` | `boolean` | Per-item override for locking width/height ratio while resizing. |
| `ariaLabels` | `IGridAriaLabels` | Per-item override, merged over the grid-wide `ariaLabels` prop and the built-in English defaults. |
| `dragAllowFrom` / `dragIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selectors restricting where a drag can/can't start. |
| `resizeIgnoreFrom` | `string \| null` | CSS selector for elements that shouldn't start a resize. |
| `dragActivationDistance` | `TDragActivationDistance \| null` | Minimum pointer movement, in pixels, before a pointerdown counts as a drag — one value for every pointer type, or distinct values per mouse/touch/pen. |
| `isBounded` | `boolean \| null` | Per-item override for restricting dragging to within the container. |
| `resizeHandles` | `TResizeHandle[] \| null` | Restricts which of the 8 resize-hint spans render/activate for this item. An empty array is a valid "no handle-driven resize" value, distinct from `isResizable: false`. |
| `isMirrored` | `boolean` | Whether this item participates in the grid's own RTL mirroring. Default `true`. |
| `enableEditMode` | `boolean` | Per-item override for the master interactivity switch. |
| `borderRadiusPx` / `useBorderRadius` | `number` / `boolean` | Per-item border radius override. |
| `showResizeHandles` / `resizeHandleColor` | `boolean` / `string` | Per-item visible resize-handle override. |
| `autoHeight` | `boolean` | Re-runs this item's own size measurement whenever its rendered content changes size. No grid-wide equivalent. |
| `moved` | `boolean` | Set internally by compaction/collision helpers to short-circuit infinite loops — not meant to be set by consumers. |
| `data` | `TMeta` | Optional, consumer-defined payload — never read or written by the library itself. Round-trips through serialize/deserialize like any other field, as long as it's JSON-serializable. |

## `TMeta` — attaching typed data to a layout item

```ts
interface IWidgetConfig {
  chartType: 'bar' | 'line';
}

const layout = ref<TLayout<IWidgetConfig>>([
  { h: 2, i: '0', w: 2, x: 0, y: 0, data: { chartType: 'bar' } },
]);
```

Attach whatever payload an item needs directly on the layout item,
instead of maintaining a parallel array keyed by `i` to look it up
separately. Every existing usage of `ILayoutItem`/`TLayout` without a
type argument keeps working unchanged — the default (`unknown`) only
matters if you actually read `.data` and want it typed as something
more specific.

The interface behind the compactor prop, its context object, and the five built-in strategies exported alongside it.

```ts
interface ICompactor {
  readonly type: string;
  compact(layout: TLayout, cols: number, context: ICompactorContext): TLayout;
}
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | A short, descriptive name for this strategy — informational only (e.g. for logging); never read by `GridLayout` itself. |
| `compact(layout, cols, context)` | Compacts a layout, **returning a new array** — must not mutate the input `layout` or any of its items in place. |

## `ICompactorContext`

```ts
interface ICompactorContext {
  compactType: ECompactType;
  minPositions?: Record<string | number, { x?: number; y?: number }>;
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `compactType` | Which built-in strategy currently applies — informational, read from `GridLayout`'s own `compactType` prop at the moment compaction runs. A custom compactor decides for itself whether/how to use this; nothing enforces it. |
| `minPositions` | Present only during a `restoreOnDrag`-gated compaction (drag end) — the pre-drag position each item shouldn't rise/shift any tighter than. Absent for every other trigger (resize end, add/remove, mount, breakpoint change, `compactNow()`/`rearrange()`), and for the two `*_OVERLAP` types. |

## The five built-in strategies

Exported individually, as a starting point for a custom compactor to
delegate back to for part of a layout (e.g. compact everything except
one pinned row) rather than reimplementing standard compaction from
scratch:

```ts
import {
  verticalCompactor,
  horizontalCompactor,
  noCompactor,
  verticalOverlapCompactor,
  horizontalOverlapCompactor,
  getCompactor,
} from '@keystone-dashboard-layout/vue';
```

| Export | Backs |
|---|---|
| `verticalCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL` (the default) |
| `horizontalCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL` |
| `noCompactor` | `ECompactType.NONE` |
| `verticalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.VERTICAL_OVERLAP` |
| `horizontalOverlapCompactor` | `ECompactType.HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` |
| `getCompactor(compactType)` | Looks up the built-in `ICompactor` matching a given `ECompactType` — the same mapping `GridLayout` itself uses internally when the `compactor` prop isn't set. |

See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/) for a
full working custom compactor, and [ECompactType](/vue/api/enums/compact-type/)
for what each built-in strategy actually does.

## `exportLayoutAsSvg`

```ts
function exportLayoutAsSvg(layout: TLayout, options?: IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions): string;
```

```ts
interface IExportLayoutAsSvgOptions {
  colNum?: number;          // default: 12
  rowHeight?: number;       // default: 150
  margin?: [number, number]; // default: [10, 10]
  containerWidth?: number;  // default: 1200 — must be supplied explicitly; see note below
  itemFill?: string;        // default: '#eef2ff'
  itemStroke?: string;      // default: '#c7d2fe'
  labelColor?: string;      // default: '#3730a3'
  backgroundColor?: string | null; // default: null (transparent)
}
```

Renders a `TLayout` as a standalone SVG string, each item drawn as a
labeled rectangle from the layout data alone — not a snapshot of
whatever's actually rendered inside each `GridItem`. Good for a
structural thumbnail of the layout itself, not a substitute for a real
screenshot of custom slot content. Never throws: an empty layout
produces a valid, empty SVG.

`containerWidth` has to be passed explicitly, unlike `GridLayout`
itself, which measures its own container automatically — there's no
DOM element for this standalone function to measure. Pass the same
width your actual grid renders at for a matching result.

The returned string is a complete `<svg>...</svg>` document — usable
directly, downloaded as a `.svg` file via a `Blob`, or drawn onto a
`<canvas>` first if a raster PNG/JPEG is specifically needed. See
[Export layout as SVG](/vue/examples/svg-export/) for a full example.

## `readOutsideDropPayload`

```ts
function readOutsideDropPayload<T>(
  dataTransfer: DataTransfer | null | undefined,
  mimeType?: string, // default: 'text/plain'
): T | null;
```

Reads and JSON-parses a native `DataTransfer` payload by MIME type —
every consumer of `allowOutsideDrop`'s `item-dropped-from-outside`
event otherwise re-implements the same `dataTransfer.getData(mimeType)`/
`JSON.parse` parsing by hand. Never throws: a missing MIME type or
malformed JSON both return `null`. Performs no runtime shape validation
against `T` — that's the caller's own responsibility, since the payload
is whatever the consumer's own drag source chose to attach.

:::caution[A real gotcha with native drag-and-drop]
`dataTransfer.getData()` only returns real values during the `drop`
event itself — not `dragenter`/`dragover`.
:::

See [outsideDropAccept & readOutsideDropPayload](/vue/examples/outside-drop-accept-payload/)
for a full working example.

Selects the built-in compaction strategy GridLayout uses via its compactType prop.

Re-exported from the package's main entry point as a real (value)
export, so you can both type `compactType` and compare/construct
against these at runtime.

```ts
enum ECompactType {
  NONE = 'none',
  HORIZONTAL = 'horizontal',
  HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP = 'horizontal-overlap',
  VERTICAL = 'vertical',
  VERTICAL_OVERLAP = 'vertical-overlap',
}
```

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `NONE` | No compaction at all — items stay exactly where placed, gaps included. Colliding items still get pushed down out of the way; this is distinct from `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` below — turning compaction off has never meant turning collision resolution off too. |
| `HORIZONTAL` | Items compact leftward, floating to the smallest available `x` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP` | Horizontal compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `x: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions entirely — matching `react-grid-layout`'s own `allowOverlap` semantics applied to compaction specifically. Items may end up visually overlapping as a result. |
| `VERTICAL` (default) | Items compact upward, floating to the smallest available `y` without colliding with anything already placed. |
| `VERTICAL_OVERLAP` | Vertical compaction, but every non-static item moves straight to `y: 0` unconditionally, ignoring collisions. Same overlap semantics as `HORIZONTAL_OVERLAP`, applied to the vertical axis. |

Replaces an older, separate `verticalCompact: boolean` prop — a single
enum-valued prop is easier to extend (the two `*_OVERLAP` members add a
capability the boolean couldn't express at all) and easier to reason
about than a growing pile of independent booleans.

See [Pluggable compaction](/vue/api/interfaces/compactor/) for the
`compactor` prop that lets you replace the algorithm entirely instead
of picking one of these five, and [Pluggable compaction (compactType &
compactor)](/vue/examples/pluggable-compaction/) for a live demo
switching between all five plus a custom compactor.

Both are exposed on the `GridLayout` instance, only meaningful with
`multiSelect` on. `alignSelected` treats the **first-selected item**
(insertion order, not an arbitrary one) as the anchor — it never moves;
every other selected item aligns to its edge or center. Needs at least
2 selected items to do anything.

`distributeSelected` needs at least 3 — the two outermost items (by
actual position, not selection order) stay exactly where they are, and
only what's "in between" spaces out evenly across the span those two
already define, the standard design-tool "distribute" behavior.

Both respect `preventCollision` when it's on — an adjustment that would
land an item on top of a *non-selected* item is skipped for that one
item; landing on another item that's *also* part of the same
align/distribute batch isn't treated as a collision at all, since
that's frequently the whole point of the command.

| Mode | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `'auto'` (default when unset) | Grows/shrinks to fit content — same as the older `autoSize: true`. In the demo above, this deliberately overflows the dashed frame, since nothing here constrains it. |
| `'fixed'` | No explicit height applied at all — the consumer's own CSS decides. Same as `autoSize: false`. |
